source: Ministry of Agriculture, Forestry and Fisheries (MAFF), General Directorate of Agriculture / ASPIRE program - Technical Document: "Sweet Corn Cultivation Techniques Resilient to Climate Change" (បច្ចេកទេសដាំដាំណាំពោតផ្អែមធន់នឹងការប្រែប្រួលអាកាសធាតុ), 2018
text:
Crop rotation: corn can be rotated with several other crop types such as morning glory/water spinach, sitting/bush beans, and gourds. The benefits of crop rotation are: maintaining soil balance, reducing fertilizer use, and reducing the spread of disease, insect pests, and other harmful factors.

Harvesting: sweet corn can typically be harvested 65-75 days after planting. Sweet corn can also be harvested about 20 days after the silk emerges. At harvest time the corn silk turns brown/dark in color while the husk remains green. A good ear of corn should have a small leaf tip remaining at least at one end of the ear. At harvest, seed corn (for replanting) should be at the stage where the kernels have hardened/dried. After the ears are picked, the corn stalks can be used as livestock feed, either by grinding or by feeding directly, or the stalks can be cut down and plowed under as green manure to increase soil fertility.

Market and seasonal considerations: the document includes a planting-and-market calendar noting the seasonal timing of land preparation, planting, and harvest activities across the year, and highlights that corn sold outside of peak harvest season/off-season commands a better price ("ខែពោតលក់បានថ្លៃ" — months when corn sells at a good price), which is a factor farmers should weigh when planning planting dates.

Business planning: farmers who intend to plant and invest in corn are advised to prepare a clear business plan before deciding to grow the crop, considering: (1) market factors (buyers) and competitors; (2) cultivation techniques; (3) investment capital needed from planting through to the first harvest; (4) various risk factors; and (5) a follow-up plan. The document provides a template business-plan table and a separate income-and-expense analysis table for sweet corn production, covering input costs (seed, chemical fertilizer, organic fertilizer, fungicide, insecticide, water pump, land-preparation labor, insect traps, plastic mulch, seedling trays, irrigation system, weeding labor, fertilizing labor, planting labor, harvest labor) versus income from the harvested output, with total profit calculated as total production income minus total production cost.
